title.title: Bounded approximation fails in a uniformly discrete free space
title.subtitle: Claim: a uniformly discrete metric space whose Lipschitz-free space has AP but no bounded AP

plain: Even when all points sit at least a step apart, approximating the space can need ever bigger tools

object.heading: Schematic: blocks $M_1, M_2, M_3, \ldots$ of points, all at mutual distance $\ge 1$

beats.text: Block $M_p$ has diameter at most $300p^2+150p+5$; the blocks sit ever farther apart
On $M_p$, every finite-rank operator of norm $\le p$ misses by at least $1/2$
Glued together: the free space has AP, but fails $\lambda$-BAP for every $\lambda$

steps: Build blocks from big graphs with random-like colourings
Anchor points force any small operator to miss by a half
Wedge the blocks together: approximation works, but not boundedly

achievement.label: Kalton's question (2004)
statement: \mathcal F(M) \text{ has AP, but fails } \lambda\text{-BAP for every } \lambda
achievement.context: Before: Smith's 2025 example did this for a discrete, not uniformly discrete, $M$
achievement.note: Corollary: an equivalent norm on $\ell_1$ that fails the metric AP

verify.detail: The block statement, the uniformly discrete $M$, and the $\ell_1$ renorming
verify.ourCheck: We read the review of the Lean statements; we did not build them

voice.text: Blocks of points at least one apart, ever farther away. Each defeats small operators.
Each block's anchors defeat small operators; wedged together, no bound survives.
Claimed: approximation works, but never with a bound.

sources.quote: a bounded uniformly discrete M_p of diameter <= 300p^2+150p+5 with finite anchors where every finite-rank operator of norm <= p errs by >= 1/2

There is a countable, unbounded, non-proper metric space with all distinct points at distance >= 1 whose real Lipschitz-free space F(M) has the approximation property but fails the lambda-bounded approximation property for every lambda.
Kalton, 'Spaces of Lipschitz and Holder functions and their applications', Collect. Math. 55 (2004)
